card.title: Introduction to Machine Learning
card.subtitle: From intuition to derivation and code implementation ‘by hand’

text.content:
This course provides the basic conceptual and technical knowledge to anyone starting out in machine learning. It begins with intuition: students first guess how the main algorithms work. Then the mathematics is thoroughly derived, step by step. Finally, the students implement the algorithms from scratch, i.e. writing the equations and the algorithmic logic in Python themselves.

From linear and logistic regression to boosted decision trees and neural networks, the goal is to show there is no magic, but beautiful (and actually simple) mathematics at play, and to give students full control over how their code is written and works.

The students learn how to assess the performance of their models and optimize them. They learn how a ROC curve is built, what under- and overfitting mean, and what the bias/variance tradeoff is, again intuitively, then mathematically. Time permitting, unsupervised techniques are covered.

For courses delivered at AIMS, the students work on a STEP, i.e. a “Study Through Exploration and Presentation.” They pick a topic they want to understand in greater depth, build a small demo (with rules on AI use so as not to delegate the thinking process), and give a 10-minute presentation in the last lecture, solo or in small groups.

Assessment combines multiple-choice quizzes, audits of the tutorials (randomly selected students are tested orally on the code they submitted), and a final exam: oral for cohorts under 40, written for larger ones.

## Testimonials  
Feedback collected from students after the course and shared with their permission.

Dr. Claire’s introduction to linear regression, decision trees, MLPs, deep neural networks, and the rigorous “pen-on-paper” session on formulating the derivatives per layer of backpropagation really drives home the point that understanding the basics gives a strong foundation for research.

card.title: Learn The Math Behind Neural Networks!
card.subtitle: It is not magical, it is mathematical

projects.page_heading: Learn The Math Behind Neural Networks!

text.content:
This day workshop is a shorter version of my 30-hour course [Introduction to Machine Learning](/teaching/intro-to-ml/), but entirely focused on neural networks. Participants get the basics (linear and logistic regression), then a thorough walk through the mathematics of forward and backward propagation. After the blackboard derivations, the second part of the workshop is a hands-on session where participants enter all equations ‘by hand’ in a Python code. They go back home with a little neural network built from scratch on a Jupyter notebook, without using any fancy ML library.

The goal is to show that the foundations behind any neural network, from simple to the latest LLM transformer, come from the simple application of the chain rule, put at scale.

images.caption: Workshop hosted in March 2023 by the University of Johannesburg Nuclear Research Centre and the Data Science Across Disciplines Research Group, both in the Faculty of Engineering and the Built Environment.

text.content:
A non-negligible feature of this workshop: it is way more fun and enriching if attendees span many ages and stages as well as disciplines and specialties. I had a blast pairing honours undergraduates with emeritus professors, both new to machine learning, for impromptu yet sparkling collaboration.

If you are interested in hosting this at your institution, please [contact me](/contact/).

card.title: Introduction to Special Relativity & Modern Physics
card.subtitle: Time, space, radiation & energy revisited

projects.page_heading: Introduction to Special Relativity & Modern Physics

text.content:
In this introduction to the theories of relativity and quantum mechanics, the relativistic concepts of space, time and energy are explained and the quantum nature of radiation and matter is discussed.


## Topics


**Special relativity**

Before Einstein · Basics of special relativity · Twin paradox and Doppler effect · Relativistic dynamics


**Modern physics**

Experimental basics of quantum theory · The particle nature of radiation · Towards a theory of the atom · Matter waves

## Testimonials  
Feedback collected from students after the course and shared with their permission.

text.quote: Prof. David is genuinely one of the best physics professors I’ve ever had. She taught me quantum mechanics in my second year of university, and I still remember how she managed to make something so confusing feel so simple and easy to understand. I’m really grateful I had the chance to learn from her, and I wish more professors shared her enthusiasm.
text.attribution: Elham Rahimi, Math Teacher in Al-Bayan Bilingual School in Kuwait

text.quote: Professor Claire David truly was one of the best professors I had the pleasure of being taught by during my undergraduate degree at York University. She cared deeply about the performance and well-being of her students both in and beyond the classroom.
text.attribution: Darren Singh, Associate Manager, Reporting and Analytics, Enterprise Risk Management

text.quote:
Fittingly for a relativity course, one of your strong points was showing perspective, the "reference frames" of different physicists, so to speak. You walked us through how classical and modern physics tackled the same problems under different conditions, so the equations made sense in context.
What stood out most, though, was how inspiring the course was. Puzzles like the twin paradox are the kind of questions that awaken curiosity, and that curiosity matters more than how easy or hard a course is, because it's what drives students to find the answers to even the hardest problems.

text.content: From its birth in the heart of the Large Hadron Collider’s detectors to its propagation and — spoiler alert — death in readout material, the course follows the journey of a particle and introduces stochastic modelling techniques with numerous hands-on sessions in Python.
